explanation: The maxillary nerve (V2) gives off infraorbital, zygomatic, and greater palatine nerves in the face, supplying the lower eyelid, cheek, and upper teeth.
modelAnswer: Infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, greater palatine nerve.

explanation: The infraorbital nerve (terminal branch of V2) gives inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, and anterior superior alveolar branches.
modelAnswer: Inferior palpebral, external nasal, superior labial, anterior superior alveolar.

explanation: The mandibular nerve (V3) gives mental and auriculotemporal branches on the face; the motor branches (masseteric, temporal, buccal) supply muscles of mastication.
modelAnswer: Mental nerve (from inferior alveolar), auriculotemporal nerve.

explanation: Muscles of facial expression develop from the second pharyngeal arch (hyoid arch), innervated by CN VII (facial nerve).
modelAnswer: Second pharyngeal arch mesoderm.

explanation: Lesion of the first somatosensory area (S1, postcentral gyrus) causes contralateral loss of fine touch, pressure, and stereognosis.
modelAnswer: Contralateral loss of fine touch, pressure, and stereognosis.

explanation: The first somatosensory area is located in the postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2) of the parietal lobe, posterior to the central sulcus.
modelAnswer: Postcentral gyrus (areas 3, 1, 2) of parietal lobe.

explanation: The second somatosensory area (S2) is located in the superior wall of the lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure), deep to the parietal lobe.
modelAnswer: Superior wall of lateral sulcus.

explanation: Area 43 (taste cortex) is located in the lower part of the postcentral gyrus near the insula, where gustatory and general sensation integrate.
modelAnswer: Lower postcentral gyrus adjacent to operculum.

explanation: Lesion of areas 5 and 7 (superior parietal lobule) causes sensory neglect of contralateral side, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.
modelAnswer: Sensory neglect, astereognosis, and optic ataxia.

explanation: The inferior parietal lobule (areas 40, 39) is located below the intraparietal sulcus, behind the lateral sulcus, comprising supramarginal and angular gyri.
modelAnswer: Below intraparietal sulcus, consisting of angular and supramarginal gyri.

explanation: Lesion of the inferior parietal lobule causes Gerstmann syndrome (left lesion): agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.
modelAnswer: Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation.

explanation: The three speech centers are Broca's area (motor speech), Wernicke's area (comprehension), and the arcuate fasciculus connecting them.
modelAnswer: Broca's area, Wernicke's area, arcuate fasciculus.

explanation: The primary motor area (M1) is located in the precentral gyrus (area 4) of the frontal lobe, anterior to the central sulcus.
modelAnswer: Precentral gyrus (area 4) of frontal lobe.

explanation: The premotor area (area 6) has a somatotopic representation similar to M1, controlling proximal and trunk muscles with less discrete localization.
modelAnswer: Similar to motor cortex but controls proximal muscles.

explanation: Lesion of area 4 (primary motor cortex) causes spastic paralysis of contralateral muscles with hyperreflexia and positive Babinski sign.
modelAnswer: Spastic paralysis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign on contralateral side.

explanation: The premotor area (area 6) is located anterior to the precentral gyrus on the lateral and medial surfaces of the frontal lobe.
modelAnswer: Anterior to precentral gyrus on lateral and medial frontal lobe.

explanation: Lesion of area 6 (premotor area) causes loss of skilled movement, motor apraxia, and rigidity without true paralysis.
modelAnswer: Motor apraxia, loss of skilled movement, rigidity.

explanation: The frontal eye field (area 8) is located in the middle frontal gyrus anterior to the premotor area, controlling voluntary eye movements.
modelAnswer: Middle frontal gyrus, anterior to premotor area.

explanation: Lesion of area 8 (frontal eye field) causes conjugate deviation of eyes toward the side of the lesion (inability to look away).
modelAnswer: Conjugate eye deviation toward the lesion.

explanation: Broca's area (speech apraxia) is located in the inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of the dominant hemisphere, usually the left.
modelAnswer: Inferior frontal gyrus (areas 44, 45) of dominant hemisphere.

explanation: Lesion of Broca's area causes expressive (motor) aphasia: non-fluent speech with good comprehension but impaired repetition.
modelAnswer: Expressive aphasia: non-fluent speech, good comprehension, poor repetition.

explanation: The supplementary motor area (SMA) is located on the medial surface of the frontal lobe anterior to the leg area of M1.
modelAnswer: Medial frontal lobe above area 4.

explanation: Lesion of SMA causes loss of spontaneous movement, speech initiation, and bilateral motor planning without paralysis.
modelAnswer: Loss of spontaneous movement and speech initiation.

explanation: Pain and temperature from the body uses three neurons: DRG (pseudounipolar), substantia gelatinosa (second order), VPL thalamus (third order).
modelAnswer: First order: dorsal root ganglion; Second order: substantia gelatinosa; Third order: VPL thalamus.

explanation: Pain and temperature from face: first order in trigeminal ganglion, second order in spinal trigeminal nucleus, third order in VPM thalamus.
modelAnswer: First order: trigeminal ganglion; Second order: spinal trigeminal nucleus; Third order: VPM thalamus.

explanation: Crude touch uses three neurons: DRG (first), nucleus proprius (second), VPL thalamus (third), ascending via anterior spinothalamic tract.
modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: nucleus proprius; Third order: VPL thalamus.

explanation: Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception sensations are carried by the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway to the somatosensory cortex.
modelAnswer: Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception.

explanation: Conscious proprioception uses three neurons: DRG, gracile/cuneate nuclei (second), VPL thalamus (third), via medial lemniscus.
modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: gracile/cuneate nuclei; Third order: VPL thalamus.

explanation: The four tracts carrying unconscious proprioception to cerebellum are dorsal spinocerebellar, ventral spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, and rostral spinocerebellar tracts.
modelAnswer: Dorsal spinocerebellar, ventral spinocerebellar, cuneocerebellar, rostral spinocerebellar.

explanation: The external arcuate fibers arise from the cuneate nucleus and carry proprioceptive information to the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
modelAnswer: Cuneate nucleus.

explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the lower limb is carried by the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (from Clarke's nucleus) to the cerebellum.
modelAnswer: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract and ventral spinocerebellar tract.

explanation: The two main extrapyramidal tracts are the reticulospinal tract (medial and lateral) and the vestibulospinal tract (lateral and medial).
modelAnswer: Rubro-spinal tract and vestibulo-spinal tract.

explanation: The olivospinal tract arises from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla and descends to the spinal cord to influence motor activity.
modelAnswer: Inferior olivary nucleus.

explanation: The lateral corticospinal tract is laminated: cervical fibers are most lateral, sacral fibers most medial, controlling progressive distal-to-proximal muscles.
modelAnswer: Cervical fibers most lateral, sacral most medial.

explanation: In the internal capsule, the pyramidal tract is arranged: anterior limb (frontal connections), genu (face), posterior limb (arm, leg) from front to back.
modelAnswer: Anterior limb: frontal; Genu: face; Posterior limb: arm above, leg below.

explanation: Extensor muscles are controlled by lateral vestibulospinal (facilitates extensors) and medial reticulospinal tracts via gamma neurons.
modelAnswer: Vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.

explanation: The tectospinal tract arises from the superior colliculus, decussates, and descends to control reflex head/neck movements toward visual stimuli.
modelAnswer: Origin: superior colliculus; Function: reflex head and neck movements toward visual stimuli.

explanation: The three arteries supplying the spinal cord are the anterior spinal artery (ventral median spinal artery) and two posterior spinal arteries.
modelAnswer: One anterior spinal artery and two posterior spinal arteries.

explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla and anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, including the corticospinal tracts.
modelAnswer: Anterior spinal artery.

explanation: Conscious proprioception uses three neurons: DRG (first order), gracile/cuneate nuclei (second order, crossing in medulla), VPL thalamus (third order), via medial lemniscus to cortex.
modelAnswer: First order: DRG; Second order: gracile/cuneate nuclei; Third order: VPL thalamus.
